concepts.name: Seismic Waves: Types, Behaviour and Diagnostic Value
key_dimensions: Distinction between P-waves (longitudinal/compressional) and S-waves (transverse/shear) — travel through solids vs. liquids
Shadow zones of P-waves (103°–143°) and S-waves (beyond 103°) and what they reveal about Earth's interior
Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) vs. body waves — slower speed, greater destruction relevance
UPSC trap: S-waves cannot travel through liquids — used to infer liquid outer core; P-waves slow down but don't stop at outer core

concepts.name: Shadow Zone of Seismic Waves: Inference about Earth's Core
key_dimensions: Geometry of P-wave shadow zone (103°–143° from epicentre) vs. complete S-wave shadow zone (beyond 103°)
Why P-waves still appear in shadow zone in weak form — refraction through outer core
What the shadow zone pattern conclusively proves about the state (solid/liquid) of the outer core
UPSC trap: the shadow zone is not a zone of no seismic activity — it is a zone of no direct wave reception

concepts.name: Layers of Earth's Interior: Composition, Depth and Physical State
key_dimensions: Crust (oceanic vs. continental), Mantle (upper and lower), Outer Core, Inner Core — depth boundaries and key minerals
Physical state of each layer: solid crust, plastic asthenosphere, solid lower mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core
Compositional differences: SIAL (crust), SIMA (oceanic crust/upper mantle), Nife (core)
UPSC trap: inner core is solid despite highest temperature — due to immense pressure; outer core is liquid

concepts.name: Discontinuities within Earth's Interior
key_dimensions: Conrad Discontinuity (within continental crust: SIAL–SIMA boundary), Mohorovičić Discontinuity (crust–mantle), Repetti Discontinuity (upper–lower mantle)
Gutenberg Discontinuity (mantle–outer core at ~2900 km) — most significant for S-wave blockage
Lehmann Discontinuity (outer core–inner core at ~5100 km)
UPSC trap: Moho is NOT a temperature boundary but a velocity/compositional boundary; depth varies under oceans (~5 km) vs. continents (~35 km)

concepts.name: Crust: Continental vs. Oceanic — Composition, Thickness and Significance
key_dimensions: Continental crust: thicker (~35–70 km under mountains), less dense, composed of granite/SIAL (Silica + Aluminium)
Oceanic crust: thinner (~5–10 km), denser, basaltic/SIMA (Silica + Magnesium), younger in age
Isostasy principle — why continents 'float' higher despite being thicker
UPSC trap: oceanic crust is denser yet thinner — hence subducts under continental crust at convergent boundaries

concepts.name: Mantle: Structure, Composition and the Asthenosphere
key_dimensions: Upper mantle (~35–700 km): includes lithosphere base and asthenosphere (~100–200 km depth) — partially molten, plastic
Lower mantle (700–2900 km): solid, denser silicate minerals under extreme pressure
Asthenosphere as source of magma and driver of plate tectonic movement — viscous flow mechanism
UPSC trap: lithosphere includes crust AND uppermost solid mantle — not synonymous with crust alone

concepts.name: Core: Outer vs. Inner Core — Composition, State and Geodynamo Theory
key_dimensions: Outer core (~2900–5100 km): liquid iron-nickel alloy — responsible for Earth's magnetic field via geodynamo effect
Inner core (~5100–6371 km): solid iron-nickel — solid due to pressure despite ~5000–6000°C temperature
Geodynamo theory: convective motion of liquid outer core generates and sustains Earth's magnetic field
UPSC trap: Earth's magnetic field originates in outer core (liquid), NOT inner core (solid); magnetic poles differ from geographic poles

concepts.name: Lithosphere vs. Asthenosphere: Boundary, Properties and Tectonic Significance
key_dimensions: Lithosphere: rigid, ~100 km thick (thicker under continents, thinner under oceans), includes crust + upper solid mantle
Asthenosphere: ductile/plastic zone in upper mantle, ~100–200 km depth, low seismic velocity zone (LVZ)
Lithospheric plates 'float' and move over the plastic asthenosphere — fundamental to plate tectonics
UPSC trap: lithosphere ≠ crust; asthenosphere is NOT liquid — it is solid but behaves plastically over geological timescales

concepts.name: Isostasy: Concept, Models and Geomorphic Implications
key_dimensions: Airy's model: crustal blocks of same density but varying thickness (mountains have deeper roots — like icebergs)
Pratt's model: crustal blocks of same thickness but varying density (mountains are less dense)
Isostatic rebound: post-glacial uplift of Scandinavia and Canada after ice sheet removal
UPSC trap: isostasy explains why high mountains have deep crustal roots — NOT that all areas are in perfect isostatic equilibrium at all times

concepts.name: Temperature, Pressure and Density Gradient within Earth
key_dimensions: Geothermal gradient: ~30°C per km in crust; rate decreases with depth — not linear throughout
Pressure increases continuously with depth due to overlying rock mass — measured in GPa at core
Density increases from ~2.7 g/cm³ (continental crust) to ~13 g/cm³ (inner core)
UPSC trap: temperature increases with depth but rate slows; inner core is solid NOT because it is cooler but because pressure overcomes melting point elevation

concepts.name: Plate Tectonics: Driving Mechanisms Rooted in Earth's Interior
key_dimensions: Convection currents in the mantle (heat from core and radioactive decay) as primary driver of plate movement
Ridge push (at divergent boundaries) and slab pull (at subduction zones) as secondary mechanisms
Role of mantle plumes (hot spots) — stationary heat sources like Hawaii, Deccan Traps formation
UPSC trap: mantle convection is the ENGINE of plate tectonics; slab pull is now considered more dominant than ridge push

concepts.name: Earth's Magnetic Field: Origin, Polarity Reversals and Significance
key_dimensions: Generated by geodynamo in liquid outer core — convective movement of iron-nickel creates electromagnetic field
Magnetic polarity reversals recorded in oceanic crust rocks — key evidence for seafloor spreading
Magnetosphere protects Earth from solar wind; its weakening linked to pole reversal transitions
UPSC trap: magnetic north pole ≠ geographic north pole; polarity reversals happen over thousands of years, not suddenly

concepts.name: Radioactivity and Heat Generation within Earth's Interior
key_dimensions: Radioactive decay of isotopes (U-238, U-235, Th-232, K-40) in crust and mantle generates internal heat
Primary heat sources: primordial heat (from accretion) + radiogenic heat — both drive mantle convection
Geothermal energy exploitation as a practical application of Earth's internal heat
UPSC trap: Earth's internal heat is NOT primarily from the core alone — significant contribution from radioactive decay in mantle and crust

concepts.name: Mohorovičić Discontinuity (Moho): Nature, Depth Variation and Significance
key_dimensions: Marks boundary between crust and mantle — identified by sudden increase in seismic wave velocity
Depth variation: ~5–10 km under oceans, ~35 km under plains, ~70 km under young fold mountains (e.g., Himalayas)
Project Mohole — failed 1960s attempt to drill through oceanic crust to reach Moho
UPSC trap: Moho depth is GREATER under thick continental crust (mountains) — inverse relationship with surface elevation due to isostasy

concepts.name: Seismology as a Tool to Understand Earth's Interior: Methods and Limitations
key_dimensions: Refraction and reflection of seismic waves at discontinuities reveal layer boundaries and material properties
Travel time curves of P and S waves used to calculate depth and velocity of internal layers
Limitations: indirect inference only; no direct sampling below ~12 km (Kola Superdeep Borehole record)
UPSC trap: our entire knowledge of Earth below 12 km is INDIRECT — based on seismic wave analysis, not direct observation

concepts.name: Volcanicity and its Connection to Earth's Interior Structure
key_dimensions: Magma originates primarily in the asthenosphere and lower crust — NOT from the outer core
Hot spots (mantle plumes) originate deep in the mantle — stationary sources that create island chains (e.g., Hawaiian chain)
Types of lava linked to crustal setting: basaltic (oceanic/divergent), andesitic (subduction zones), rhyolitic (continental)
UPSC trap: volcanoes at divergent and subduction boundaries have different magma compositions due to different depths/sources of melting

concepts.name: Evidence for Earth's Layered Structure: Convergence of Multiple Disciplines
key_dimensions: Seismological evidence: wave velocity changes, shadow zones, travel time anomalies
Meteorite analogy: iron meteorites correspond to core composition; stony meteorites to mantle/crust
Moment of inertia calculations suggesting mass concentration toward centre — consistent with dense core
UPSC trap: no single method alone proves layered structure — UPSC may ask about the 'most conclusive' evidence (seismology) vs. supporting evidence

concepts.name: Gutenberg Discontinuity: Significance and What it Reveals
key_dimensions: Located at ~2,900 km depth — boundary between lower mantle and outer core
S-waves completely stop here (cannot pass through liquid outer core) — proves outer core is liquid
P-wave velocity drops sharply here before increasing again — refraction creates P-wave shadow zone
UPSC trap: Gutenberg discontinuity is the most seismically significant boundary — more diagnostic than Moho for understanding core state

concepts.name: SIAL, SIMA and NIFE: Compositional Zones and Their Geomorphic Relevance
key_dimensions: SIAL (Silica + Aluminium): upper continental crust, density ~2.7 g/cm³, granitic composition
SIMA (Silica + Magnesium): oceanic crust and upper mantle, density ~3.0 g/cm³, basaltic composition
NIFE (Nickel + Iron): core composition, density ~10–13 g/cm³
UPSC trap: SIMA underlies BOTH oceanic crust AND continental crust (below the SIAL layer) — SIAL is absent under ocean floors

concepts.name: Earth's Interior and Earthquake Focus: Shallow, Intermediate and Deep Focus Earthquakes
key_dimensions: Shallow focus (0–70 km): in crust/lithosphere — most frequent and most destructive (e.g., most Himalayan earthquakes)
Intermediate focus (70–300 km): upper mantle zone along subducting slabs
Deep focus (300–700 km): occur in subducting lithospheric slabs within mantle — Benioff Zone
UPSC trap: deep focus earthquakes CANNOT occur below 700 km because the subducting slab assimilates into ductile mantle — rocks lose rigidity needed for brittle fracture
